newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Credit Suisse first-half net jumps 70 percent.
newsitem.headline: Credit Suisse first-half net jumps 70 percent.

text.p: Credit Suisse Group, reporting its half-year results early due to merger plans, said preliminary figures showed net profit surged 70 percent to around 1.41 billion Swiss francs ($933 million) in the first half of 1997.

CS Group released the figures on Monday two weeks ahead of schedule as part of an announcement that it plans to merge with Swiss life and non-life insurer Winterthur. Under the deal, Winterthur would continue to operate as an independent entity.

"Half-year results have benefited from very favourable financial markets, the weakness of the Swiss franc against the dollar, and the initial stages of the Group's domestic reorganisation," it said in a statement.
It said full and final figures for the six months would still be released as planned on August 27.
Net profit growth was at the high end of growth estimates, which had run between 45 and 90 percent.

The results were overshadowed by the merger plan on the Swiss stock exchange, where CS shares jumped three percent to 215 Swiss francs before falling back to around 203 at midday, 5.50 francs or 2.6 percent below the prior close.

Credit Suisse was the second big Swiss bank to report on the half year after Union Bank of Switzerland , which last week posted a jump of 67.4 percent in net profit to a 1.856 billion Swiss francs. Swiss Bank Corp is due to report on Wednesday, with net profit also forecast to rise by 50 to 70 percent.

"Overall I don't view the numbers as a major surprise. I'd say they are consistent with UBS with the exception that the trading problem that UBS had in London was a one-off," said John Leonard at Salomon Brothers in London. UBS injected a note of disappointment for markets by saying its trading results were flat due to losses in equity derivatives trading.

Credit Suisse's statement said that the net profit, after minority interests and implementation of a new credit risk management framework, was equal to about 7.25 Swiss francs per share. It estimated return on equity for the half year at about 17 percent.
Net operating income was up 26 percent at approximately 8.050 billion Swiss francs.
"Strong revenue growth was experienced in all categories of income," CS said.
The cost/income ratio was expected to improve to 66.9 percent for the half year from 69.8 percent for the full year 1996.
Personnel expenses as a percentage of net operating profit were estimated to be 47 percent as against 47.5 percent for full year 1996.
Total expenses, including a provision of 25 million for the proposed merger, were 5.050 billion Swiss francs.

CS did not provide a comparative figure for operating expense, but said the amount was up "due mainly to higher incentive performance bonus accruals in the trading divisions and the effect of a stronger dollar." ($ = 1.511 Swiss Francs)
